raw_response.headline_result_summary: Using a municipality-level difference-in-differences design combined with multinomial probit propensity-score kernel matching across 2000-2010 in rural Brazil, Barde (2017) finds that small-scale rural water supply systems implemented, operated, and maintained by participatory community-based water user associations (+assoc) increased rural household access to piped water on premises by 6.58 percentage points more (0.0658***, SE = 0.0161 with municipal clustering; 0.0658**, SE = 0.0271 with state clustering; N = 1,899 observations across 1,008 municipalities) than non-participatory small-scale rural systems implemented and operated by local governments (+loc). Descriptively, rural piped water coverage rose from 16.0% to 33.4% (+17.4 pp) in water user association municipalities versus 15.3% to 24.9% (+9.6 pp) in local government project municipalities, and in full-sample covariate-adjusted DiD regressions local government projects alone did not outperform municipalities with no new rural project (+loc = 0.00662, SE = 0.00614, null), whereas WUA projects did (+assoc = 0.0667***, SE = 0.00987). Within local government project municipalities, however, rural access gains rose significantly when external accountability mechanisms were present—prior social-group requests for water (+0.0793***), municipal user participation mechanisms (+0.0409**), tighter 2004 mayoral electoral competition (victory margin = -0.150**), and local TV (+0.104***) or radio (+0.0408*) stations—whereas these political/media variables were all null in WUA municipalities, supporting higher built-in accountability as the mechanism behind participatory WUA success.
raw_response.specification_or_coding_pitfalls:
1. Comparator / exposure pole orientation (+assoc vs. +loc vs. no change): The headline model (Table 4) codes participatory community-based water user association governance (+assoc = 1) against non-participatory local municipal government rural provision (+loc = 0), yielding +0.0658***. If a synthesis instead treated municipal/public local government provision (+loc) as the focal intervention, its effect is negative relative to WUAs (-0.0658***) and statistically null relative to no rural project once covariates are included (+loc = 0.00662, SE = 0.00614, Table 12 col. 3, attenuating from unadjusted 0.0107* / 0.0123** in cols. 1-2).
2. Dropped minus-sign glyphs in PDF text extraction + inverse polarity of victory margin: Across the Elsevier PDF tables (Tables 5, 6, 10, 11, 12), Unicode minus signs were dropped in text extraction. Critically, in Table 6 Panel A cols. 3-4 (PDF p. 11), 'Margin 2000' and 'Margin 2004' extract as '0.0580' and '0.150**', whereas the prose on PDF p. 12 explicitly states: 'As expected, both coefficients are negative: the larger the distance in victory between the mayor and its competitor, the lower the access rates increase.' Moreover, because higher victory margin means LESS electoral competition, the negative coefficient (-0.150**) on victory margin implies a POSITIVE (favorable_to_access) effect of political competition.
3. State-level clustering in unweighted vs. kernel-matched DiD: In unweighted full-sample DiD with <=27 state (UF) clusters (Table 12 col. 4), +assoc vs. 'no change' has p < 0.10 (0.0667*, SE = 0.0347), whereas in the primary kernel-matched DiD with UF clusters (Table 4 col. 3: 0.0658**, SE = 0.0271) and unweighted +assoc vs. +loc with UF clusters (Table 12 col. 6: 0.0795**, SE = 0.0309) it remains significant at p < 0.05.
4. Borderline significance for local radio: In Table 6 Panel A col. 5, 'Local radio station' is 0.0408* (SE = 0.0204), marked with a single asterisk (*, 10% level), whereas 'Local tv station' is 0.104*** (1% level).
5. Bundled mixed-provider category: Municipalities where both a WUA and a local provider added rural systems (256 municipalities in 2008/2010, Table 2; p. 13 n.9) are grouped into '+assoc' (author reports results are unchanged if separated).
raw_response.study_design: Panel difference-in-differences (2000 and 2010 censuses linked to 2000 and 2008 national water/sanitation surveys, PNSB) combined with multinomial probit propensity-score kernel matching (Heckman, Ichimura, & Todd 1997, 1998; Lechner 2001), informed by 36 semi-structured qualitative interviews and supplemented with urban falsification, 1990-2000 pre-trend placebo, and subgroup accountability-channel DiD regressions.
raw_response.unit_and_sample_size: Brazilian municipalities (specifically rural areas of municipalities, plus urban areas in falsification check). Primary kernel-weighted DiD (Table 4, cols. 1-3): 1,899 municipality-year observations across 1,008 municipalities (bootstrapped means test col. 4: N = 955). Descriptive comparison (Table 1): 4,892 municipalities (3,717 no change, 592 +loc government, 583 +WUA). Unweighted full-sample DiD (Appendix Table 12): 10,448 observations across 5,389 municipalities (unadjusted, cols. 1-2), 9,928 observations across 5,344 municipalities (with covariates, cols. 3-4), and 2,168 observations across 1,161 municipalities (+assoc vs. +loc, cols. 5-6). Accountability channel DiD subsamples (Table 6): 947-962 observations across 520-522 local-government-project municipalities (Panel A) and 950-963 observations across 506-507 WUA-project municipalities (Panel B).
